descripcion_es: Actions in progress at a future moment (will be doing) and actions completed before that moment (will have done).
resumen: The future continuous (will be + -ing) describes something that will be in progress at a future moment; the future perfect (will have + past participle) describes something that will already have finished before that moment.

filas: This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Rome.
By Friday we'll have finished the report.
In May she'll have been working here for ten years.

explicacion.texto: Future continuous: an action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future (at 8 tomorrow, this time next week). It is equivalent to Spanish “estaré haciendo”.

It is also used for plans that will happen in the normal course of events and to ask about plans politely: Will you be using the car tonight? (asking whether you are going to use the car tonight, without putting pressure on you).

Future perfect: an action that will be completed before a future moment. It is equivalent to Spanish “habré hecho”. It often goes with by (by, no later than), by the time (when, by the moment that) or in + period.

items: By + date = Spanish “para”, not “por”: by next year (Spanish “para el año que viene”).
By the time + present simple: By the time you arrive, I'll have left (not “will arrive”).
The future perfect continuous stresses the duration up to a future point: for + period.
State verbs (know, own, believe) are not usually used in the continuous form: By June I'll have known her for a year.

ejemplos.frase: Don't call me at nine; I'll be having dinner.
ejemplos.traduccion: No me llames a las nueve; estaré cenando.

ejemplos.frase: By the end of the month, the company will have hired forty new staff.
ejemplos.traduccion: A finales de mes, la empresa habrá contratado a cuarenta empleados nuevos.

ejemplos.frase: Will you be going past the post office later?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Vas a pasar por correos más tarde?

ejemplos.frase: By the time the film starts, we'll have eaten all the popcorn.
ejemplos.traduccion: Para cuando empiece la película, nos habremos comido todas las palomitas.

ejemplos.frase: Next year they will have been married for twenty-five years.
ejemplos.traduccion: El año que viene harán veinticinco años de casados.

ejemplos.frase: This time next week I'll be lying on a beach in Crete.
ejemplos.traduccion: La semana que viene a estas horas estaré tumbado en una playa de Creta.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: By the time you will arrive, I will have left.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: By the time you arrive, I will have left.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: After by the time, when, before or until you use the present, not will.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Tomorrow at this time I will work in the garden.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Tomorrow at this time I will be working in the garden.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “estaré trabajando” at a specific moment in the future requires the future continuous, not will + infinitive.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: For next Friday I'll have finished.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: By next Friday I'll have finished.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “para” + deadline is translated by, not for.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the future continuous or the future perfect.
ejercicios.frase: At 11 tomorrow morning I ___ (sit) an exam, so I can't help you.
respuestas: will be sitting
'll be sitting
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's rule on the future continuous applies: an action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future (Spanish “estaré haciendo”). The clue is At 11 tomorrow morning, an exact time, and the consequence so I can't help you: at that moment I will be busy in the middle of the exam. The form is will be + sitting (or 'll be sitting). Sit an exam is the British expression for “to take an exam”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Action in progress at a specific future moment: future continuous.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mañana a las 11 estaré haciendo un examen, así que no puedo ayudarte.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will sit
errores_previstos.explicacion: Will sit presents the exam as a future fact as a whole; to say that I will be in the middle of it at that time you need will be sitting.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will have sat
errores_previstos.explicacion: The future perfect would indicate that by 11 I will already have finished it, the opposite of what the sentence says.

errores_previstos.respuesta: am sitting
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present continuous would express a plan, but with a specific time at which the action is in progress the card requires will be + -ing.

glosario.significado: hacer un examen, presentarse a un examen (inglés británico)

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the future continuous or the future perfect.
ejercicios.frase: By 2030 the city ___ (build) a new metro line.
respuestas: will have built
'll have built
ejercicios.explicacion: The future perfect rule applies: an action that will be completed before a future moment, Spanish “habré hecho”. The clue is By 2030; as Rules and key points reminds you, by + date means Spanish “para”, that is, at the latest on that date. The form is will have + past participle: will have built (or 'll have built). Build is irregular and its past participle is built.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: By + date indicates something completed before that moment: future perfect.
ejercicios.traduccion: Para 2030 la ciudad habrá construido una nueva línea de metro.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will build
errores_previstos.explicacion: The future simple does not express that the work will be finished before 2030; with by + date you use will have built.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will be building
errores_previstos.explicacion: The future continuous would indicate that in 2030 it will still be under construction, not that it will have been finished.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will have builded
errores_previstos.explicacion: Build is irregular: the past participle is built.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb.
ejercicios.frase: By the time we ___ (get) to the station, the train will have left.
respuestas: get
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in Rules and key points applies: by the time + present simple. In time clauses that refer to the future (by the time, when, before, until) English uses the present, never will. The clue is By the time at the beginning of the gap; the future is already in the main clause (will have left). That is why the form is get, in the present, just as Spanish uses the subjunctive “lleguemos” and not the future.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After by the time you use the present simple, not will.
ejercicios.traduccion: Para cuando lleguemos a la estación, el tren ya se habrá ido.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will get
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the typical error listed on the card: after by the time you use the present, not will.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will have got
errores_previstos.explicacion: The time clause does not take the future perfect; the present simple get is enough.

errores_previstos.respuesta: got
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past does not fit, because the arrival is in the future; you use the present get.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the future perfect continuous.
ejercicios.frase: In September I ___ (teach) at this school for twenty years.
respuestas: will have been teaching
'll have been teaching
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in Rules and key points applies: the future perfect continuous stresses the duration up to a future point with for + period. The clue is the combination In September (the future point) and for twenty years (the accumulated duration). The form is will have been + teaching. Spanish expresses this with “hará veinte años que…” or “llevaré veinte años dando clase”, structures that cannot be translated word for word.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Duration up to a future point with for: future perfect continuous.
ejercicios.traduccion: En septiembre hará veinte años que doy clase en este colegio.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will teach
errores_previstos.explicacion: The future simple does not express the duration accumulated up to September; with for + period you need will have been teaching.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will be teaching
errores_previstos.explicacion: The future continuous only says that I will be teaching at that moment, without the idea of the twenty accumulated years.

errores_previstos.respuesta: am teaching
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present does not place the duration at a future point; the rule requires will have been + -ing.

respuestas: will be sleeping
ejercicios.explicacion: The future continuous rule applies: an action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future. The clue is after midnight, the reference moment, and the implicit reason for the advice: at that time we will be fast asleep and the call would wake us up. That is why the form is will be sleeping, equivalent to Spanish “estaremos durmiendo”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: At that time we will be in the middle of sleeping: future continuous.
ejercicios.traduccion: No llames después de medianoche. Estaremos durmiendo.

por_opcion.will sleep: Incorrect in this context: it presents sleeping as a future fact, but it does not convey that the call would interrupt us in the middle of our sleep.
por_opcion.will be sleeping: Correct: future continuous for an action in progress at a future moment.
por_opcion.will have slept: Incorrect: it would indicate that by that time we will already have finished sleeping, which makes no sense here.

ejercicios.frase: I hope the builders ___ the roof by the time winter comes.
respuestas: will have repaired
ejercicios.explicacion: The future perfect rule applies: an action completed before a future moment. The clue is by the time winter comes, which sets the deadline, and the meaning of the sentence: the speaker wants the repair to be finished before winter. The form is will have repaired. Note that winter comes is in the present, as by the time requires.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Something completed before a future moment: future perfect.
ejercicios.traduccion: Espero que los obreros hayan arreglado el tejado para cuando llegue el invierno.

por_opcion.will be repairing: Incorrect: it would indicate that they will still be repairing it when winter arrives, exactly what is not wanted.
por_opcion.will have repaired: Correct: future perfect; the repair will be finished before the deadline.
por_opcion.had repaired: Incorrect: the past perfect looks at the past and does not fit a future deadline.
por_opcion.are repairing: Incorrect: the present continuous expresses a plan or an action in progress, not something completed before winter.

glosario.definicion_l: a substance added to soaps or detergents to increase their cleansing action · a person who creates a business or who organizes and develops a country

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the most polite question for asking about plans.
ejercicios.frase: ___ the printer this afternoon? I need to print some tickets.
respuestas: Will you be using
ejercicios.explicacion: The polite use of the future continuous explained on the card applies: Will you be + -ing asks about someone's plans without putting pressure on them or asking for anything directly (as in Will you be using the car tonight?). The clue is the context: I want the printer, but instead of asking for it I tactfully ask whether the other person needs it. The form is Will you be using.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Will you be + -ing asks about plans without putting pressure on someone or asking for anything directly.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Vas a usar la impresora esta tarde? Necesito imprimir unas entradas.

por_opcion.Will you be using: Correct: polite future continuous for asking about plans without putting pressure on someone.
por_opcion.Will you have used: Incorrect: it would ask whether you will have finished using it before a deadline, which is not what is being asked.
por_opcion.Will you have been using: Incorrect: the perfect continuous measures a duration up to a future point and makes no sense here.

ejercicios.frase: Please send me the figures ___ Thursday at the latest.
respuestas: by
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in Rules and key points applies: by + date is equivalent to Spanish “para”, that is, a deadline. The clue is at the latest, which confirms that it is a deadline. That is why the preposition is by. It is one of the most frequent errors made by Spanish speakers, who tend to translate “para” as for.
ejercicios.traduccion: Por favor, envíame las cifras para el jueves como muy tarde.

por_opcion.by: Correct: by marks the deadline, “by Thursday at the latest”.
por_opcion.for: Incorrect: it is the calque of Spanish “para”; for with a date indicates destination or purpose, not a deadline.
por_opcion.until: Incorrect: until indicates that something lasts up to that moment (“until Thursday”), not a deadline for delivery.

ejercicios.frase: By the time you will read this letter, I will have left the country.
respuestas: By the time you read this letter, I will have left the country.
By the time you read this letter, I'll have left the country.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in Rules and key points applies: by the time + present simple. In the time clause will is not used even though it refers to the future; the future goes only in the main clause (I will have left). The clue is By the time at the beginning. Will have left or the contraction 'll have left are accepted, because both are the same future perfect.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In the time clause with by the time you use the present, not will.
ejercicios.traduccion: Para cuando leas esta carta, me habré ido del país.

errores_previstos.respuesta: By the time you will read this letter, I will have left the country.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: after by the time you use the present, not will.

errores_previstos.respuesta: By the time you read this letter, I will leave the country.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It corrects the time clause but spoils the main clause: the leaving will be completed before, so you need will have left.

errores_previstos.respuesta: By the time you will have read this letter, I will have left the country.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It puts the future perfect in the time clause; after by the time the present simple is enough.

ejercicios.frase: By next summer I will be knowing her for ten years.
respuestas: By next summer I will have known her for ten years.
By next summer I'll have known her for ten years.
ejercicios.explicacion: Two rules in Rules and key points apply: state verbs (know, own, believe) are not usually used in the continuous form, and a duration up to a future point with for is expressed with the future perfect. The clue is By next summer + for ten years, together with the verb know. As know does not take -ing, the simple form is used instead of the future perfect continuous: will have known.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Know is a state verb and this is a duration up to a future point: will have known.
ejercicios.traduccion: El próximo verano hará diez años que la conozco.

errores_previstos.respuesta: By next summer I will be knowing her for ten years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: know is a state verb and the duration up to a future point requires will have known.

errores_previstos.respuesta: By next summer I will have been knowing her for ten years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It uses the continuous form with a state verb; know goes in the future perfect simple.

errores_previstos.respuesta: By next summer I will know her for ten years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The future simple does not express the duration accumulated up to the summer.

ejercicios.frase: For the end of the week we will have painted the whole house.
respuestas: By the end of the week we will have painted the whole house.
By the end of the week we'll have painted the whole house.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in Rules and key points applies: by + date = Spanish “para”, not “por”, together with the card's typical error For next Friday instead of By next Friday. The clue is that the complement indicates a deadline for finishing something (will have painted). That is why For must be changed to By; the rest of the sentence, in the future perfect, is already correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “para” with a deadline is translated by.
ejercicios.traduccion: Para el fin de semana habremos pintado toda la casa.

errores_previstos.respuesta: For the end of the week we will have painted the whole house.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: Spanish “para” + deadline is translated by, not for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Until the end of the week we will have painted the whole house.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Until expresses duration up to a moment, not a deadline for completion; you need by.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In the end of the week we will have painted the whole house.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the end means “finally, eventually”; the deadline is expressed with by.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence using the future perfect with by + the time given.
ejercicios.frase: The meeting will finish before six o'clock. (by six o'clock)
respuestas: The meeting will have finished by six o'clock.
The meeting'll have finished by six o'clock.
By six o'clock the meeting will have finished.
By six o'clock, the meeting will have finished.
ejercicios.explicacion: The future perfect rule applies: something completed before a future moment, with by. The clue is the instruction by six o'clock, which replaces before six o'clock. The sentence takes will have + past participle: The meeting will have finished by six o'clock. The contraction and the order with By six o'clock at the beginning are also accepted, because the time expression can go first.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Something completed before a future moment is expressed with will have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: La reunión habrá terminado a las seis.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The meeting will finish by six o'clock.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It does not use the future perfect that the exercise requires; the action completed before a deadline is will have finished.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The meeting will have finish by six o'clock.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After will have comes the past participle: finished.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The meeting will have finished for six o'clock.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The deadline is expressed with by, not with for.

ejercicios.frase: They will have finished the work by Monday.
respuestas: They will not have finished the work by Monday.
They won't have finished the work by Monday.
ejercicios.explicacion: The negative form of the future perfect applies: the negation goes after will, as in all tenses with will. The clue is the instruction to make the sentence negative and the verb will have finished. The result is will not have finished or, contracted, won't have finished; have and the past participle do not change.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The negation goes after will: won't have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No habrán terminado el trabajo para el lunes.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They will have not finished the work by Monday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It puts not after have; the negation goes right after will: won't have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They don't will have finished the work by Monday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Will is a modal and is not made negative with do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: They haven't finished the work by Monday.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present perfect does not place the deadline in the future; you need won't have finished.

respuestas: This time next week I'll be skiing
I'll be skiing this time next week
ejercicios.explicacion: The future continuous rule with a specific moment in the future applies: this time next week is one of the expressions the card gives as a signal. The words form the time expression this time next week and the verb I'll be skiing (will be + -ing). The time expression can go at the beginning or at the end, which is why both orders are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Time expression + future continuous: I'll be skiing.
ejercicios.traduccion: La semana que viene a estas horas estaré esquiando.

errores_previstos.respuesta: This next week time I'll be skiing
errores_previstos.explicacion: It breaks up the fixed expression this time next week (Spanish “a estas horas la semana que viene”).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'll skiing be this time next week
errores_previstos.explicacion: It changes the order of the verb; the form is will be + -ing: I'll be skiing.

respuestas: they will have landed by then
by then they will have landed
ejercicios.explicacion: The future perfect rule with by then (Spanish “para entonces”) applies, one of the typical signals for this tense. The words form the subject they, the verb will have landed (will have + past participle) and the complement by then, which can go at the end or at the beginning. That is why both orders are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Will have + past participle with by then.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they have will landed by then
errores_previstos.explicacion: It swaps will and have; the fixed order is will have + past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: they will have by then landed
errores_previstos.explicacion: It separates the auxiliary from the past participle with the time complement, which is not done here.

descripcion_larga_es: The future continuous (will be + -ing) presents an action in progress at a future moment, Spanish “estaré haciendo”; the future perfect (will have + past participle) presents it as already completed before that moment, Spanish “habré hecho”. They are essential for talking about deadlines, forecasts and schedules. Spanish speakers find it particularly hard to translate “para” with a deadline (by, not for) and to avoid putting will after by the time.

contexto.que_es: They are two future tenses with aspect. The future continuous (will be + -ing) places the listener in the middle of a future action; the future perfect (will have + past participle) looks back from a future point and sees the action as already completed. The future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing) stresses the duration up to that point.
contexto.por_que_importa: They allow you to talk precisely about deadlines and timetables (By 2030 the city will have built…), something constant in reports, projects and economic policy. The future continuous also lets you ask politely about someone else's plans without seeming to ask them for something. Confusing the two changes the message: “I'll be finishing” is not “I'll have finished”.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: The future continuous appears with specific moments (at 11 tomorrow, this time next week). The future perfect appears with by + date, by the time, by then or in + period, and the perfect continuous with for + duration. Spanish speakers often translate “para el viernes” as for Friday instead of by Friday, and put will after by the time by calque of the Spanish future, when English requires the present.
